The Age of Agents: How does it change commerce and how we pay?

A century ago, the department store created the first great retail revolution. eCommerce decoupled shopping from physical location and upended retail business models. m-Commerce blurred the lines between physical and digital. Each of these revolutions left a wake of creative destruction. We are now on the cusp of the next big upheaval in commerce - the one driven by Agents. In its first phase, we are already increasingly becoming adept at product search and price comparisons through AI chatbots. In the next phase, agents will likely execute complex workflow and cross-app tasks for us (e.g., nudge, plan and action a party). Eventually, we may see a world of agent-to-agent transactions where agents can plan, execute and negotiate (e.g., discounts) on our behalf. This means profound changes in and implications for the payments and commerce sectors. With this note, we are kicking off a cross-sector Bernstein series on Agentic Commerce.
Hype or reality? A bit of both right now. On one hand, a growing portion of consumers are using AI tools for product search and research (with the primary use-case being price comparison). On the other hand, it hasn’t made a dent on how commerce is being done. Etsy offers a high watermark with \~30% of referral traffic coming from AI chatbots, but it still represents <1% of total web traffic. Even with the new shopping features, we’re much more in the realm of conversational search than true Agentic Commerce. It’s early days.
The real transformation happens when Agents become capable of planning and executing ‘autonomously’ on our behalf. That needs work on the models’ capabilities, trust in these models, governance frameworks, and merchant infrastructure. An example would be an Agent nudging and planning ahead for a birthday party including calling & booking the venue, scanning email & sending invites, brainstorming to select a theme, and ordering party supplies. In a future scenario, the agent could also negotiate on our behalf e.g., specific discounts. This would be a true step-change in the shopping experience.
Agents may bring profound changes in commerce, can usher in an era of hyperpersonalization, unlock long tail of merchants, potentially accelerate the growth of eCommerce (with the room for market to expand around high consideration categories) - and also materially change how we pay. Agents may initially ‘influence’ verticals such as low-value goods, apparel, groceries, ticketing and eventually evolve into high consideration purchases around travel and luxury, etc.
Just like in the early days of the internet - there is currently a lot of experimentation. Several protocols (e.g., for agent communication, payments, autonomous agents) have been being introduced by Google, Open AI/Stripe, Visa and Coinbase.
For payments, trust and governance become paramount (& challenging) in the agentic era. Cards (not alternative methods) likely emerge as winners in the near/medium term. The concern for eCommerce marketplaces is the risk of disintermediation — and ultimately what this means for the flow of ad dollars and switching costs. We do note that shifts in consumer behavior will take time, and we will monitor the speed of this change. In the interim, incremental, high-converting traffic from AI is a near-term positive.

INVESTMENT IMPLICATIONS
U.S. PAYMENTS
Trust and governance become paramount (and challenging) in the Agentic Commerce era (more so than m-Commerce or eCommerce). Traditional commerce is designed with humans in the loop. In a world where agents are roaming around on the internet filling out forms and buying things, there are several questions with regard to trust (how do we know an agent is a good agent), programmability of transactions, authentication (e.g., in Europe with 2FA), user consent and intent, dispute management, fraud mitigation, charge back management, audit trail, optimization of different payment methods, personalization and standards/technology fragmentation.
It is likely that cards emerge as winners in the Agentic era given that Agents pose new challenges in ‘trust, governance and standards’ – something the networks do extraordinarily well at. The same is likely true for new-age processors such as Stripe (private) & Adyen. Potentially accelerated eCommerce growth is typically good for the networks (more market share, more VAS). Agentic Commerce also means potentially more VAS around security, consent, programmability, dispute management (and token proliferation, also personalization tokens?). While there are certain protocols that can eventually dilute the role of networks (e.g., Google AP2, Coinbase (covered by Bernstein) x402 e.g., cryptography vs. tokens debate) – V/MA will likely retain control of governance/standards. It is also possible that we see accelerated transaction growth due to baskets being split across different merchants as agents optimize products, deals etc.
Tokens have been the key enablers of successfully taking the 60-yr old card construct into the digital age. Just like what Apple Pay did to cards, AI agents may end up solidifying the utility/moat of cards. Can you imagine bank payments or subscale domestic schemes having advanced authentication, fraud controls, programmable limits, or personalization? eCommerce accelerated cash digitization and value-added services growth (more token enablement, enhanced security and data needs).
Optionality for B2B? Agentic commerce can reshape the entire B2B value chain by using sourcing agents and purchasing bots, that can not only enable automation of vendor selection, purchase orders (depending on pre-set business requirements), reconciliation, optimization of working capital (using virtual cards), but also drive faster procurement processes.
Digital Wallets are in a more un-chartered territory — on the one hand, if Agents are handling our payments — do we really care about the ‘guest checkout’ friction? On the other hand, two-sided wallets such as PayPal can expand their value proposition (around trust, protections, fraud/disputes), and also help consumers dynamically find savings, rewards, personalization, payments optimization (e.g., on BNPL, credit/debit cards) as a two-sided network. PayPal’s strategic partnership with Google here is quite interesting to watch. Card issuers maybe in a tricky spot eventually. Imagine a world where our AI assistant recommend the right card for the right purchase and optimizing rewards to the nth degree — takes competition to a whole new level.
Key developments to watch: New Agentic Models (including cross-platform and agent-to-agent transactions), Merchant adoption, Evolution of protocols (Google’s AP2, Stripe-Open AI’s ACP, Visa Intelligence Commerce, Mastercard Agent Pay, Visa’s Trusted Agent Protocol), Visa-AWS partnership on Agentic.
Risks to watch: Agent consolidation (vs. fragmentation), governance problems can be solved by LLMs – although it will be hard to enforce with V/MA controlling liability shift/interchange for cards. Stablecoins can be used initially in micro-payments, and build from there? In a long-term scenario of agent-to-agent negotiated transactions, it is possible that ‘agents’ negotiate on cheaper rails and optimize payment methods.
US INTERNET
We expect Agentic AI to accelerate eCommerce growth in the long-run, with room for the online market to expand given current penetration rates of 15-16% — particularly for higher consideration categories where consumers will benefit from better search results, better comparability across marketplaces, and more personalized results - areas where a personal assistant or in-store SA play a major role in sales conversions. The concern for eCommerce marketplaces is the risk of disintermediation if consumers increasingly start their search and discovery process on third-party chatbots — and ultimately what this means for the flow of ad dollars and switching costs between eCommerce platforms. We do note that shifts in consumer behavior will take time, and we will continue to monitor the speed of this change and whether it benefits

U.S. ONLINE TRAVEL AND LODGING
AI Agents already exist in the wider leisure space, with Google’s AI agent capable of booking restaurant tables and tickets without a human having to navigate to the booking site. Both Google and OpenAI (private) have suggested this is also coming for flight/hotel bookings in time. The key questions now are (1) is agentic commerce going to be dominated by the top of the funnel player (Google, OpenAI) or will consumers use agentic tools on vertical specific platforms, (2) where will top-of-funnel agents be able to make that final booking, will it be solely possible on major brands or OTAs or is this an opportunity to disintermediate these platforms, and (3) what effect will this have on the advertising/paid placement revenues at the OTA level if agents rather than humans are making the final purchase.
We have framed the debate in recent notes including the potential end game for OTAs (OTAs and AI: Existential threat or opportunity of a lifetime?), their potential bull case (OTAs: What is the AI Bull Case? What might make us believe it?),, and admission by OTA CEOs that travel bookings could be better in an AI world (irbnb & Booking: The Internet broke travel, can AI fix it? CEOs at the Skift Forum) and a note that sets out how channel changes shift winners (Weekend Consumer Blast: From Cursus Publicus to Teletext Holidays to AI, who will win in the next travel channel?).
In online travel, we would expect greater protection if the content being sold is proprietary/unique/less sophisticated and prefer Airbnb over Booking /Expedia for this reason.

DETAILS
We are at the beginning of a new era in commerce - the agentic one. In its first phase, we are already increasingly becoming adept at product search and price comparisons through AI agents. In the next phase (possibly 2026 or 2027), it's possible that we have agents who are executing complex workflow and cross-app tasks for us. Eventually, we may see a world of agent-toagent transactions where agents can plan, execute and negotiate on our behalf. This means profound changes in the payments and commerce infrastructure. With this note, we are kicking off a cross-sector Bernstein series on Agentic Commerce.
Hype or reality? A bit of both right now. On one hand, a growing portion of consumers are using AI tools for product search and research (with the primary use-case being price comparison).
As per Visa’s recent survey, \~47% consumers have already used AI for at least one shopping-related task in the US (Exhibit 1), with price comparison being the most compelling application of AI tools. Within the \~47%, 21% used it for gift ideas, 16% used them to conduct product research, 15% used it for search and 11% used it to try out products online within virtual fitting rooms / other tools.
Mastercard’s survey conducted with 4,000+ consumers, 42% were using AI tools for their holiday shopping. Many were open to let AI handle buying gifts in order to avoid stress. Some of the most popular use cases include getting personalized product recommendations, confirming the best deal before completing a purchase, and summarizing thousands of reviews quickly.
As per Adobe, AI agent-driven traffic grew 800%+ during Black Friday. Further, Salesforce (covered by Bernstein) reported that global online sales driven by AI agents at \$14.2B globally this year (\$3B in the US; 17% of US online sales). Amazon saw total website sessions increase 20% yoy, those where Rufus was involved grew 35% yoy.
• Unlike prior tech cycles (e.g., eCommerce which took decade+ for infrastructure build), AI agents can navigate existing infrastructure – meaning faster deployment.

Even with the new shopping features, we’re much more in the realm of conversational search/commerce than true Agentic Commerce. It’s early days.

AI will start to shift from being used mainly in the discovery phase to selection and purchase phases. Apparel, groceries, marketplaces verticals could be at the forefront - i.e. verticals where AI can quickly review and compare a lot of similar products across merchants. Next, could be the ticketing vertical (e.g. movie, concert tickets) where agents can add value by incorporating users’ scheduling needs. Then, comes the travel vertical (e.g. hotels, transportation) where AI solves for complexity. Lastly, further down the road, agentic commerce can add value through true high consideration purchases (e.g. in case of luxury goods, automotive, etc.).

THE REAL TRANSFORMATION HAPPENS WHEN AGENTS BECOME CAPABLE OF PLANNING AND EXECUTING ‘AUTONOMOUSLY’ ON OUR BEHALF.
For e.g., for tasks such as:
• Scanning emails for a birthday party invite, adding it to calendar and then nudging the user to order gifts along with suggestions
• Finding a recipe on TikTok, tweaking it and ordering ingredients
• Plan trips, find hotels and restaurants as per preferences, followed by looking up the best deals, planning the day and finding the best flights.
THE LONG-TERM POSSIBILITY IS AGENT-TO-AGENT HYPER-PERSONALIZED TRANSACTIONS
...where Agents negotiate on behalf of consumers. Agents will then personalize pricing based on loyalty and consumer demand, with retailers considering ‘Agents’ not just humans for marketing purposes. Agents will also then proactively recommend payment methods and negotiate on behalf of consumers e.g. negotiate bulk discounts with seller’s agent on furniture sale and delivery or bundled hotel + flight pricing with a travel agent.
Anytime there are paradigm shifts, new winners and losers emerge.
CAN AGENTS ACCELERATE THE GROWTH OF ECOMMERCE?
Agents may bring profound changes in commerce, can usher in an era of hyper-personalization, unlock long tail of merchants, potentially accelerate the growth of eCommerce - and also materially change how we pay. Card market growth has historically been closely tied to the growth of eCommerce - eCommerce has both higher card and valueadded services penetration (i.e. richer growth and yields).
The current eCommerce model prioritizes search-order vs. truly customized recommendations. We find current commerce experiences sometimes tiring and often putting the burden of product research onto the consumer. Agentic can help with long-tailed merchant discovery, insights on products and customized/tailored cross-platform experiences which have been evasive on search-based eCommerce. Agentic commerce has the potential to uncover product discovery in a way an experienced in-store assistant at a department store would do.
• It is also possible that we see accelerated transaction growth due to baskets being split across different merchants as agents optimize products, deals etc.
THE BEGINNING OF AN ERA MARKED BY A LOT OF EXPERIMENTATION
Google recently released several new AI-powered shopping updates including conversational queries in AI Mode in Search as well as Gemini App (helps quickly decide what to buy based on price, reviews, available inventory), AI ‘Call Store’ feature (to find products in-stock nearby), Agentic checkout (for completing purchases at pre-set price limits) with eligible merchants. In Sep’25, OpenAI released its Checkout System with integrations with Shopify, Etsy, Walmart, etc. OpenAI also released its Shopping Research a tool that generates personalized buyer’s guides for consumers during the holiday season, by asking clarifying questions in a quiz format, and curating answers based on reviews from high-quality websites (incl. Reddit). Perplexity and PayPal launched Instant Buy ahead of holiday shopping season, which enables PayPal merchants to be discoverable within Perplexity, and allow consumers to checkout within chat (see link).

• Data Communication Protocol
• Anthropic launched the Model Context Protocol or MCP in Nov’24 aimed at creating a universal standard for connecting AI models to external data sources/tools. MCP allows AI systems to connect to any data source without needing custom integrations ie/ replacing fragmented integrations with a single protocol. Block has been an early adopter here.
• Commerce Protocols
• Small Steps (compatible with existing models, infrastructure and human initiated):
• OpenAI launched its new agentic commerce protocol (ACP) in collaboration with Stripe in Sep 2025. ACP is “new open standard codeveloped by Stripe and OpenAI that enables programmatic commerce flows between buyers, AI agents, and businesses. It provides a blueprint for how businesses can make their checkouts agent-ready so that customers using AI agents, such as ChatGPT, can buy products directly from where they’re discovering them.” With ACP, merchants don’t need to do much work on their back-end to enable Agents (can do via a simple API) and can use their existing payments processor for agentic payments.
• The medium and long-term oriented (autonomous agents):
• Google announced its Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) also in September, an open protocol to enable agent-led payment transactions across platforms. AP2 also supports stablecoins and cryptocurrencies. Unlike’s OpenAI/Stripe’s ACP protocol (which optimizes checkout for agents and human initiated/authenticated transactions), Google’s AP2 is designed for a fundamentally different autonomous agent workflow which raises questions around user authorization, intent, and accountability. It solves this by cryptographic mandates around user intent and authorization. The AP2 protocol can be used as an extension of the Agent2Agent Protocol and Model Context Protocol (MCP). It is interesting that AP2 tries to solve by ‘cryptographically secured’ mandates what V/MA enforce through tokens and governance. While Google has Mastercard, Amex, PayPal and Adyen as partners - its possible (and likely) the company figures out a way to partner with Visa.
• Wild Card:
• Coinbase launched x402 in collaboration with Cloudfare in May 2025. x402 brings back the dormant HTTP 402 code (payment required) and combines it with Stablecoins to enable instant, global, micropayments on the internet (i.e. putting a money layer protocol on the internet). The idea is that agents essentially get a stablecoin wallets for internet native micro-payments e.g., a dataset, image, software, compute, API access - i.e. make high frequency/low value payments possible for autonomous agents. Given the largely non-existent usage of stablecoins for payments and in B2B systems today, unclear KYC/AML framework and the economic model, we view this as a wildcard currently.
• Identity/Trust Protocols
• Visa introduced its Trusted Agent Protocol in October 2025, a framework for Agentic Commerce that helps secure communication between merchants and AI agents. The protocol will address unique challenges merchants face with the advent of Agentic Commerce around managing bot detection systems, supporting agent-driven checkout and preserving visibility into the underlying customers. Trusted Agent Protocol will use agent-specific cryptographic signatures which will include information about agent intent (i.e. if an agent is a trusted agent for a specific purchase), consumer recognition (data to indicate whether customer has an existing account with the merchant), and payment information. Visa’s Trusted Agent Protocol complements Open AI/Stripe’s Agentic Commerce Protocol - the latter more focused on the payment token and information transfer between the agent and merchant vs. Visa’s protocol aimed at solving for trust between agent/merchants and preserving merchant visibility into the underlying customers.

Mastercard also launched its Agentic Payments Program, Agent Pay in Apr’25, aimed at delivering smart, more secure and personal payments experiences to consumers, merchants and issuers. Mastercard introduced Agentic tokens, which are built on Mastercard’s existing tokenization capabilities that power global commerce, contactless payments, Mastercard Payment Passkeys, recurring expenses and subscriptions. Agent Pay is based on key 4 components: 1) Securely registering and authenticating trusted agents, 2) Facilitating safe and secure transactions (enhanced tokenization tech, 3) clear rules for consumer control and 4) Protecting against fraud and supporting consumer disputes.

Source: Bernstein analysis MERCHANTS ARE CAUTIOUSLY APPROACHING THE AGE OF AGENTS Merchants are cautiously approaching the age of agents with Walmart, Target, Etsy, Shopify partnering with OpenAI while Amazon blocking AI agents. For merchants agentic raises profound questions on consumer loyalty, ad revenues, infrastructure and product design. While Agents have the potential to bring in more traffic, merchants are also worried about disintermediation (including on the data), brand recognition. integration challenges across different standards, fraud and compliance. Below are some recent developments with regards to large merchants/marketplaces. Etsy has been an early mover in the space through its Instant Checkout integration with ChatGPT. This integration is an opportunity for Etsy to punch above its weight on traffic acquisition through this newer channel. With a longer tail of niche inventory and higher consideration purchase occasions, conversational search queries with more context help. eBay has created its own unified commerce platform that is enabling a fully connected experience between its internal AI Shopping Agent (piloted in May’25) as well as third-parties such as OpenAI, which provides shoppers personalized suggestions based on real-time listings. eBay’s own shopping agent provides personalized product suggestions and expert guidance to consumers, based on their preferences. The company’s rich data history coupled with unique product listings could help eBay compete more effectively on search in an AI-first world. Companies like Wayfair have noted that it is crucial for its specialized product catalog to be integrated and accurately represented on search platforms (e.g. Google, Perplexity, OpenAI). The company is optimizing its listings to rank well in AI search results and working towards making its catalog fully transactable. As it relates to onsite capabilities, Wayfair is iterating upon search (using LLMs to move beyond traditional keyword matching) and introducing new tools for consumers to visualize its catalog better (e.g., Muse an AI discovery feed and Complete Deluxe as a complete the room/look feature with shoppable content powered by AI). Walmart has its own AI Assistant Sparky, that helps customers explore new products, plan purchases (e.g. for a birthday party) and complete their weekly purchases. Sparky is based on a mental model whose data foundation builds on Walmart’s own ecosystem (product and service catalog) and customer data. Over time, customer activity i.e. understanding customer intent, discovery, execution and post purchase experience will continue to feed into the model and help the Agent understand customers better and serve their needs more effectively. 11 on 10-Dec-2025 Harshita Rawat, CFA    +1 917 344 8485  harshita.rawat@bernsteinsg.com 9 December 2025 US PAYMENTS AND INTERNET BERNSTEIN|SOCIETE CENERALECROUP

Amazon has its own agent Rufus, which it believes continues to get better and is used more broadly. Amazon also has the ‘Buy for Me’ feature which allows consumers to view items not stocked by Amazon, but available with other merchants which has also been successful for them. Over time, Amazon expects to partner with third-parties, similar to how search engines began many years ago. More recently, news came out that Amazon has put in place measures prohibiting bots from other companies (i.e. ChatGPT, Perpexlity, Google, Meta, Huawei (private), Mistral (private), etc.), in order to protect its advertising revenue (chatbots and tools help bypass advertisements), promote its own AI ecosystem (i.e. Rufus), to have more control over pricing and customer experiences as well as for security and fraud prevention.
For Shopify more channels brings more complexity for merchants (an area of Strength for Shopify). Shopify has working on developing the infrastructure required to enable Agentic Commerce and currently has some key products for including: 1) Catalog (launched in 2q for product discovery, aimed at giving AI partners and shopping apps real-time access to products on Shopify’s merchant network globally), 2) Universal Cart (that helps add carts from various stores in one spot within the chat, that helps consumers track the items they want to buy), 3) Checkout Kit (already used by Microsoft Copilot; enables merchants to embed checkout in their agent). Shopify also has tools for merchants such as Sidekick, that helps them run core parts of business (e.g. analytics, SEO automation, etc.) and so far has seen \~750K merchants using sidekick with \~100M conversations in Oct’25 alone. Shopify has also partnered with OpenAI, where merchants will be able to sell directly into ChatGPT.
Target announced (in Nov’25) the launch of a conversational and curated shopping experience within ChatGPT. Consumers will be able to purchase multiple items in a single transaction and select fulfillment options. As per the company, customers will soon also be able to request personalized recommendations, browse and build shopping baskets and make purchases seamlessly through their account.

Trust and governance become paramount (and challenging) in the “A-commerce” era (more so than m-Commerce or eCommerce). Traditional commerce is designed with humans in the loop. In a world where agents are roaming around on the internet filling out forms and buying things, many issues/questions emerge with regards to:
• How do we program a transaction to be within certain parameters?
• How does the infrastructure manage delegated consent and user intent?
• How are transactions authenticated - whether it is a legitimate transaction in the first place? How do we do 2-factor authentication, how do we perform biometrics-based enhanced authentication?
• How do we manage disputes?
• How do we optimize for different payment methods (yes, many people choose payment methods based on the types of purchases)?
• What happens in the event of fraud? Who is liable for what (the merchant, consumer, merchant’s agent, consumer’s agent or the LLM)? How is the audit trail managed?
• Bots are usually ‘bad’. How do merchants know that an agent is a good/verified agent?
• How do we personalize to get the best experience from Agents?
• How do merchants navigate the fragmentation of protocols and unclear governance frameworks?
WITHIN PAYMENTS, CARDS LIKELY EMERGE AS ‘WINNERS’
Networks appear to be the winners. Same is likely true for new-age processors such as Stripe & Adyen. Digital Wallets are in a more unchartered territory — on the one hand, if Agents are handling our payments — do we really care about the ‘guest checkout’ friction? On the other hand, two-sided wallets such as PayPal can expand their value proposition and help consumers dynamically find savings, rewards, personalization and trust as a two-sided network. PayPal’s strategic partnership with Google here is quite interesting and one to watch. Card issuers maybe in a tricky spot eventually. Imagine a world where our AI assistant recommends the right card for the right purchase and optimizing rewards to the nth degree — takes competition to a whole new level.
• Potentially accelerated eCommerce growth is typicallly good for the networks (more market share, more VAS). Remember cash/local payment methods are (typically) less likely to have market share online.
• Agentic Commerce also means more transactions and potentially more VAS around security, consent, programmability, dispute management (and token proliferation, potentially also personalization tokens?).
• Agentic Commerce poses new challenges in ‘trust, governance and standards’ – something the networks do extraordinarily well. Domestic Schemes and other payment methods likely can’t keep up.
• While there are certain protocols that can eventually dilute the role of networks (e.g., Google AP2, Coinbase x402 e.g., cryptography vs. tokens debate) – V/MA likely retain control of governance/standards. Remember, Apple was faced with a similar decision 12 years ago with Apple Pay. We all know how that played out..
Tokens have been the key enablers of successfully taking the 60-yr old card construct into the digital age. Just like what Apple Pay did to cards, AI agents may end up solidifying the utility/moat of cards. Can you imagine bank payments or sub-scale domestic schemes having advanced authentication, fraud controls, programmable limits, personalization?
Optionality for B2B? Agentic commerce ‘can’ reshape the entire B2B value chain by using sourcing agents and purchasing bots, that can not only enable automation of vendor selection, purchase orders (depending on pre-set business requirements), reconciliation, optimization of working capital (using virtual cards), but also drive faster procurement processes. It’s possible that this drives adoption of cards - although its currently unclear.

RISKS TO WATCH
• Governance problems can be solved by LLMs (dimnishing the role played by V/MA)– although will be hard to enforce with V/MA controlling liability shift/interchange for cards.
Stablecoins can be used initially in micropayments.. and build from there? We note that if the payments' infrastructure were being created from scratch, then stablecoins could have been a good fit for Agentic payments with their programmability, ability to do micro-transactions & 24x7 global infrastructure. But payments infrastructure already exists and there is a huge last mile problem for any new payment method across 100m+ merchant locations and 8b consumer credentials. Plus stablecoins currently lack governance rules (without which eCommerce payments don’t work) which were developed for cards over decades.
• Agent consolidation (vs. fragmentation) - consolidation in other parts of the value chain is likely not good for the payments ecosystem.
• In a long-term scenario of agent-to-agent negotiated transactions, it is possible that ‘agents’ negotiate on cheaper rails and optimize payment methods although unclear what the consumer value proposition will be.
Although cards feel quite ready and well-positioned for the agentic era - we are watching the battles currently being fought to own protocols, align partnerships, etc. PayPal is an interesting player (potentially under-appreciated - jury is out) to monitor in this context, and we wonder if the company can reverse its decline in relevance in the current eCommerce model with a value proposition of trust, protections (buyer/seller), payments optimization (e.g., on cards, BNPL, offers) and personalization in the agentic model.
